description: Team Earth2Orbit is a collective of student developers and researchers where I, alongside my team, focus on bridging the gap between Earth and space exploration. Our project is dedicated to identifying and analyzing terrestrial locations that serve as direct analogs for permanent Moon and Mars base sites. By combining software engineering, technical solutions, and scientific research, we build tools to model and study extraterrestrial environments right here on Earth.
summary:
ORBITAL — Earth Analog Explorer is an interactive web app that helps people find and evaluate places on Earth that resemble permanent Moon base locations and Mars. Users explore a 3D model of the Earth, Moon, Mars and Sun, then browse a catalog of 13 Earth sites, 8 lunar and 10 Martian reference locations. They can filter Earth sites by eight traits (aridity, cold, impact geology, volcanism, lava caves, isolation, robotics testing, astrobiology) and target body.

Each analog is backed by NASA, JPL or ESA sources, and every entry states its limits. Where evidence is missing, the app shows “no data” instead of guessing. Users can compare up to three sites side by side. They can also submit a new candidate site, which is checked against live NASA POWER climate data.

The project addresses the challenge by turning scattered analog research into a transparent, searchable tool. It is important because it separates documented evidence from assumptions, which helps students and researchers see where Earth can, and cannot, stand in for other worlds.
details:
What it does.

  • 3D explorer. A Three.js scene shows the Earth, Moon, Mars and Sun. Users select a world and click location markers to open details, photos (NASA imagery with credits) and a map.
  • Analog catalog. Search, target filter (Moon/Mars) and trait filters work together, and all selected traits must match. Each site has a status: documented analog, landscape data only, or needs verification. Today 7 sites are documented analogs (e.g., Atacama, Devon Island, Antarctic Dry Valleys, Hawaiian lava fields, Mojave, Iceland, Lanzarote), 1 has landscape data only (Wadi Rum) and 5 are marked as needing verification.
  • Evidence comparison. A table for up to 3 sites shows confirmed traits and gaps. The number of marks reflects the amount of confirmed evidence, not a “similarity score” or suitability for a base.
  • Candidate analysis. Users enter coordinates, a target body and declared traits. The server fetches NASA POWER climatology (temperature, precipitation, solar radiation). It labels aridity (< 1 mm/day) and cold (< 0 °C) as “measured” by project thresholds. Geological claims stay “declared, unverified”. Candidates are saved in the browser and can be exported as JSON.
  • ORI guide. A bilingual (Ukrainian/English) assistant answers questions only from the project’s data and says plainly when it has no answer. It can run commands such as “add Atacama and Namib to comparison” or “create a candidate…”. It has a 3D avatar and browser speech output. An optional LLM mode (OpenAI API) is off by default and needs a server-side key.

Benefits and intended impact. The app makes analog science approachable for students and early-stage researchers. It builds data literacy by showing where evidence is strong and where it is missing, and it gives a starting point for proposing new field-test sites.

Tools and technologies.

  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, Three.js (3D scene, OrbitControls), Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles for the Earth map.
  • Backend: Node.js (22+) HTTP API with input validation, request-size limits, origin checks, rate limiting and a 24-hour climate cache with request de-duplication.
  • Data: NASA POWER API, NASA/JPL/ESA articles, NASA Image Library, NASA Blue Marble and Solar System Scope textures.
  • Browser APIs: localStorage, Web Speech API.
  • Testing and deployment: Node’s built-in test runner for the API and guide logic. GitHub Pages hosts a static version, where the API handlers run in the browser. A full Node version is deployable on Railway.

Creativity. The project combines a cinematic 3D space view, a scientific evidence table and a conversational guide that can operate the interface. Its most distinctive choice is scientific honesty: unknown values are never filled in, fill values from NASA are treated as “unknown” (0 stays a real measurement), and the guide refuses to invent answers.

Factors the team considered.

  • An analogy is not proof of suitability. Every site lists its limits, such as different gravity, atmosphere or biology.
  • POWER data is a regional climate norm, not an on-site measurement.
  • Coordinates are approximate, and some points are regional landmarks.
  • Accessibility and language: the interface is Ukrainian and English, and a photo map is shown when WebGL is unavailable.
  • Security and privacy: no API keys in client code, and user candidates stay in the browser.
  • Image and texture credits are shown in the app.
